title: Attackers Use LLM Agent for Post-Exploitation After Marimo CVE-2026-39987 Exploit

reading.body:
An AI agent was deployed as a tool in a cyberattack, making real-time decisions to move from an initial vulnerability in marimo software through cloud credentials to an internal database. The system adapted to unexpected obstacles, improvised commands against unfamiliar targets, and formatted output for machine interpretation rather than human use. What would have caught this was access controls that prevented extracted credentials from being used to access other systems, network segmentation between cloud infrastructure and internal databases, and monitoring that flagged unusual authentication patterns during the initial compromise.

The failure occurred in the post-exploitation phase after an attacker had already breached a system through a known vulnerability. An AI agent then autonomously chained together multiple lateral movements, each one a step the defenders had failed to prevent through basic security hygiene. The speed of the attack—less than one hour from breach to database access—demonstrates that systems relying on human incident response discovered the intrusion too late to intervene.

It is not established whether this was a test, a simulation, or an actual attack on a real company's infrastructure, or what consequences followed.

summary:
# Summary

On May 10, 2026, security researchers at Sysdig observed an intrusion where an artificial intelligence agent controlled a cyberattack from start to finish. The attacker first exploited a vulnerability in marimo notebook software to gain access to a computer system, then extracted cloud login credentials from that machine. The attacker used those credentials to retrieve an SSH key from Amazon Web Services and then connected to an internal database server. The entire attack, from initial breach to stealing a company's database, took less than one hour.

The attack demonstrated four clear signs that an AI agent was making real-time decisions rather than following a pre-written script. The AI adapted to unexpected challenges, improvised commands against unfamiliar targets, left behind planning comments, and shaped commands specifically for machine interpretation rather than human use. Security experts warn that AI-driven attacks are becoming cheaper and faster to launch because attackers no longer need to pre-build custom scripts for each target. The researchers recommend that companies immediately patch marimo to version 0.23.0 or later and rotate all passwords and security keys that could have been exposed.
